item.description:
Covers come out clearer: smooth by default, accents that always show, and a paper option that lets the art take over.

  • Covers are smooth now. The paper grain is a Texture slider in a category's Theme tab, off unless you want it.
  • Accents always stand out from their colour, so patterns, lines and shapes stay visible on small covers and on the shelf.
  • New in the Colour tab, Printed on: your colour (as before), Paper (a pale paper with the art and titles in your colour), or Both, with books taking turns.
  • Advanced → Title colour: automatic, light, dark, the accent, or a colour of your own, for titles, authors and spines.
  • Spines can be printed with the cover's art, like a paperback, or plain cloth, like a hardback. Choose in the Theme tab.
  • Picking a layout shows it on the preview straight away, so you can see each one as you add it.
  • Justified stack runs its art full-bleed behind the title instead of cropping it under a hard edge.
  • Titles are always plain text on top of the cover: the blurred patch behind titles on busy patterns is gone. Labels, panels and bands belong to the layouts that have them.
  • On a busy pattern (tartan, patchwork, marbling, cut-outs and the like), the Layout tab marks the layouts that give the title its own ground as Reads best.

A new category editor: pick a colour off a paint card, a theme and layouts, and watch a shelf of books change as you do.

  • Editing or creating a category opens a wide editor: the options on the left, a live preview on the right.
  • Colour: pick one of thirteen colour families, then a shade from its paint card (each with its own name, like Snooker Baize), and set its strength. Mix your own… has sliders for colour, brightness and strength, plus the fourteen 2.0 palettes as old favourites.
  • Choose an accent (tonal, contrast, gold or cream) and how far books stray from the colour across the shelf: matching, sibling shades, or pale to deep.
  • Theme: every pattern, grouped as Classic, Maps, Botanical, Repeats, Scenes and Objects, drawn in your colour.
  • Layout: every title layout shown on a real book. Pick one, several to take turns, or any.
  • The preview shows one book, a shelf or a wall of them, each book its own roll of the settings. Try another title shows how long titles fit; Surprise me rolls a whole new look.
  • Right-click any cover or spine to Shuffle Cover (undoable) or Choose Cover… from six others.
  • Settings → Categories shows each category's look and opens the editor.
  • Existing categories keep exactly the covers they had.

Forty-one more cover themes: pressed flowers, tartans, star charts and printed objects that fill themselves in.

  • Nine botanical themes, each piece growing its own plants: pressed flowers, engraved plate, cyanotype, night umbels, Arts & Crafts repeat, mid-century flat and stamped cloth, plus a seed packet and a herbarium sheet.
  • Seed packet: the title in the packet’s band, the flower and SOW month from when you saved the piece, READ from its length and BY from its author.
  • Herbarium sheet: a taped specimen with a label giving the title, collector (the author), category and the day you saved it.
  • Eight repeat themes, each piece with its own pattern: wave pattern, patchwork quilt, tartan, terrazzo, Bauhaus grid, op-art moiré, marbled boards and halftone.
  • Ten scene themes: linocut, ridgelines, strata section, star chart, transit diagram, figure-ground plan, architect’s elevation, paper cut-outs, moth plate and crease pattern.
  • Mineral specimen: a crystal cluster on felt with a museum card giving the title, author, category and the day you saved the piece.
  • Thirteen printed objects that fill themselves in from the piece: airmail envelope (postmarked the day you saved it), card ticket (the fare is the reading time), catalogue card, exercise book, typescript, crossword (the title crossed with the author’s surname), chess problem, patent drawing, matchbox, score (the melody spelled from the title), tarot card (the sun, moon or star when the title names one), pulp paperback and wood-type specimen.
  • Every new theme dresses its spines to match: a strip of its pattern, or the object’s own colours.
  • Titles set straight onto the busiest themes get a soft veil behind them, so they stay readable.
